terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to write tonight's log entry.

tasks.title: Write down where
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `radio_log.py`, make a variable called `location`: the hill, a comma, a space, the word `grid`, a space and the grid reference, like this:

```
Scarth Fell, grid NY 4127 0836
```

Print it to see it. Check runs your file with other hills and grid references in place of the ones at the top and reads `location` after the lines under `# Task 1`.
nextSteps: Read tonight's callout near the top of the file.
Join `hill`, the text in the middle and `grid_ref` with `+`.
Check the spaces: `+` adds none of its own.
Print it and compare it with the task.
hints: Three pieces of text go together: the hill, the words in the middle, and the grid reference.
`+` joins text exactly as it is, so the comma and both spaces have to be inside the quotes of the middle piece.
The line has the shape `location = hill + "..." + grid_ref`, with the comma, the word grid and their spaces in the quotes.

tasks.title: Tidy the call sign
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, make a variable called `clean_call_sign`: the call sign in `call_sign` without the spaces at its start and end, in capital letters, like this:

```
BRAVO TWO
```

Print it to see it. Check tries call signs with spaces around them, without any, and with a capital already in them.
nextSteps: Run the file once with `print(call_sign)` to see the spaces.
Find the method in the lesson that removes them.
Find the one that turns text into capitals.
Use both, one after the other, and print the result.
hints: Two things change: the spaces at the ends go, and the letters become capitals.
Methods are written after the text with a dot and round brackets. You can write a second one straight after the first.
The line has the shape `clean_call_sign = call_sign.strip()....()`, with the capitals method where the dots are.

tasks.title: Write the crew line
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, make a variable called `crew_line`: the text `Crew out:`, a space, then the number in `crew_out`, like this:

```
Crew out: 6
```

Print it to see it. `crew_line` must be text. Check tries other crews, including nobody at all.
nextSteps: Try joining the text and `crew_out` with `+` and read the error.
Read the part of the lesson about text and numbers.
Turn the number into text before you join it.
Print it and run the file.
hints: `crew_out` is a whole number, and `+` cannot join text to a number.
Python has a way to turn a number into text. The lesson shows it next to the TypeError.
The line has the shape `crew_line = "Crew out: " + str(...)`, with the crew's name where the dots are.

tasks.title: Write the log entry
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, make a variable called `log_entry` with an f-string: the clean call sign, the word `to`, the location, the word `with`, the number in `crew_out` and the word `crew`, with one space between each, like this:

```
BRAVO TWO to Scarth Fell, grid NY 4127 0836 with 6 crew
```

Print it to see it. Check starts Task 4 from `clean_call_sign` and `location` as Tasks 1 and 2 should make them, with other callouts, and reads your file to see that `log_entry` is made with an f-string.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on f-strings.
Write the entry as one text in quotes, with an `f` in front.
Put each variable's name in curly braces where its value goes.
Print it and compare it with the task word by word.
hints: An f-string lets you write the whole line as you want it to read, with the names where their values go.
Put an `f` right before the opening quote, and each name inside `{` and `}`. A number needs no turning into text there.
The line has the shape `log_entry = f"{clean_call_sign} to ... crew"`, with the location and the crew in braces in the middle.
